summary.title: The Absolute Minimum Every Software Developer Must Know About Unicode in 2023 (Still No Excuses!)
summary.one_liner: Unicode code points, UTF-8/UTF-16/UTF-32 encodings, and extended grapheme clusters explain why string length, comparison, and case conversion break, and why you should use a Unicode library and normalize strings.
keywords: what is unicode in plain english
why does string length differ between languages
takeaways: Unicode maps characters to code points; encodings like UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32 store those code points as bytes.
Do not count bytes or code points as characters; iterate over extended grapheme clusters, using a current Unicode library such as ICU.
Normalize strings (NFC/NFD and compatibility forms) before comparing or searching, since visually identical strings can differ in bytes.
Unicode rules for grapheme clusters change roughly yearly, so library versions matter.
Case conversion and rendering can depend on locale, e.g. Turkish dotless i.
summary.summary: This long-form article by Tonsky updates Joel Spolsky's 2003 essay on encodings for 2023. It explains what Unicode is, how code points are allocated and how UTF-8, UTF-16 and UTF-32 encode them, and why byte counts and code point counts are poor proxies for characters. It then covers extended grapheme clusters with many examples across languages and emoji, normalization forms, locale dependence, and surrogate pairs, closing with a checklist of practical rules.
